data.summary: Aerospace and mechanical engineering student at UTEP (minor in Materials Science) researching laser powder bed fusion of NASA's GRX-810 oxide-dispersion-strengthened superalloy at the W.M. Keck Center for 3D Innovation. My work connects build angle and machine to microstructure and room-temperature tensile properties after HIP, toward process qualification across EOS L-PBF systems. I also founded a student hardware R&D lab and design manufacturing solutions in industry.

research.title: Microstructure–Property Relationships in GRX-810 NiCoCr ODS Alloy Fabricated via Laser Powder Bed Fusion: A Multi-System, Build Angle and Machine-Dependent Study
research.org: UTEP W.M. Keck Center · NASA Marshall Space Flight Center · NASA Glenn Research Center
research.question: How do build angle and EOS L-PBF machine affect the microstructure and room-temperature tensile properties of HIP-treated GRX-810?
methods: Five EOS L-PBF systems (M280-M1, M280-M2, M290, M400-M1, M400-M2) on a NASA MSFC build artifact
Room-temperature tensile tests of miniature dog bones at 45°, 50°, 60°, 75° and 90° build angles
Optical microscopy (glyceregia electro-etch), EBSD (IPF maps, pole figures), SEM fractography
keyFindings: On all three machines tested so far, mean UTS was lower at 90° than at 45°.
EOS M280-M1: 884.6 MPa mean UTS at 45° vs 793.8 MPa at 90° (10.3% lower).
Machine-to-machine differences and scatter in yield strength, especially at 75° and 90°.
Columnar grains along the build direction in the sections examined; dimpled fracture surfaces at 45° indicate ductile failure.
Preliminary: the mechanism (retained anisotropy after HIP) and a texture–strength link are not yet confirmed.
nextSteps: Statistical analysis of machine × angle effects
Evidence for GRX-810 qualification across EOS machines
